title: Biomechanical and physical determinants of bowling speed in cricket: a novel approach to systematic review and meta-analysis of correlational data
author: Ramachandran AK, Singh U, Connor JD, Doma K
notes: 18 studies. Pooled correlations with ball release speed: overall biomechanics r=0.42, overall physical characteristics r=0.65; run-up speed r=0.50; front knee angle at release r=0.40; front knee angle at front-foot contact r=0.26; total arm length r=0.65; shoulder strength r=0.58; CoM velocity at release and vertical GRF not significant. Correlational, not causal. DOI 10.1080/14763141.2020.1858152. Abstract only.

title: Technique Variables Associated with Fast Bowling Performance: A Systematic-Narrative Review
author: Bhandurge S, Alway P, Allen S, Blenkinsop G, King M
notes: 15 studies 2000-2022. Consensus: faster run-up; efficient sequential transfer of linear to angular momentum; quick deceleration in the delivery stride with an extended front knee from front-foot contact to release; delaying the bowling arm. Other variables conflicting/limited. Abstract read via Crossref (publisher page blocked).

title: Relationships between fast bowling technique and ball release speed in cricket
author: Worthington PJ, King MA, Ranson CA
notes: 20 elite male fast bowlers; 4 technique variables explained 74% of release-speed variation: faster run-up, straighter front knee through front-foot contact, more upper-trunk flexion before release, delayed onset of arm circumduction. DOI 10.1123/jab.29.1.78. Abstract only.

title: Technique factors related to ball release speed and trunk injuries in high performance cricket fast bowlers
author: Portus MR, Mason BR, Elliott BC, Pfitzner MC, Done RP
notes: 42 AIS high-performance fast bowlers over 4 years. Faster bowlers: extended front knee during front-foot contact, higher/faster braking and vertical impact forces, maximum hip-shoulder separation reached LATER in the stride, larger shoulder rotation to release. More front-on shoulders at back-foot contact -> more shoulder counter-rotation. Lumbar stress fracture group had higher counter-rotation (p=0.01); back-injured bowlers showed 'mixed' technique characteristics. Abstract via Europe PMC.

title: The velocity dependence of techniques commonly linked with lower back injury in cricket fast bowling
author: Middleton K, Chauhan P, Elliott B, Alderson J
publisher: ISBS Conference Proceedings (27th International Conference on Biomechanics in Sports)
notes: 17 high-performance bowlers, fast/normal/slow deliveries. NO association between velocity and shoulder counter-rotation or front-knee flexion; velocity associated with trunk lateral flexion and max hip-shoulder separation (together ~11% of variance for normal deliveries at ~31.3 m/s). Conference abstract.

title: The Athletic Profile of Fast Bowling in Cricket: A Review
author: Johnstone JA, Mitchell ACS, Hughes G, Watson T, Ford PA, Garrett AT
publisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 28(5):1465-1473
notes: Elite fast bowlers 36-40.5 m/s (129-146 km/h), 'express' >146 km/h (citing Glazier 2000, n=9). Run-up length r=0.70 with delivery speed; run-up speed may account for up to 16% of release speed; faster final 5 m of run-up r=0.72; run-up velocity ~17-21.6 km/h, ~22 km/h in last 5 m. Straighter front knee (>150 deg) linked to speed but front-foot impact 5-9x body mass absorbed by soft tissue and lower back; eccentric lower-body strength may help hold the knee. Elite bowlers 1.83-1.92 m tall. GPS: ~22 km per multi-day day, ~13 km ODI, ~5.5 km T20. Accepted manuscript read in full.

title: Anthropometric and strength correlates of fast bowling speed in junior and senior cricketers
author: Pyne DB, Duthie GM, Saunders PU, Petersen CA, Portus MR
publisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 20(3):620-626
notes: 24 first-class seniors (23.9 y) peak speed 126.7 km/h vs 48 junior representative bowlers (14.8 y) 99.6 km/h. Junior speed predicted by static jump, bench throw, body mass, % muscle, height (r=0.86); seniors by static jump and arm length (r=0.74). Abstract via Europe PMC.

title: The effects of a four weeks combined resistance training programme on cricket bowling velocity
author: Maker R, Taliep MS
publisher: South African Journal of Sports Medicine 33(1)
notes: 18 adult male CLUB pace bowlers (1st/2nd division), baseline 87-91 km/h. 2x/wk for 4 wk alongside nets: bodyweight squats 2x10-12, hip raises 2x10-12, split squats 2x6-8, med-ball chest pass/overhead slam/rotational throws 2x6-8, 1 min rest, plus over/underweight balls (+/-10-15%). +5.1 km/h (~6%) vs 0 in control; accuracy unchanged; no injuries reported. n=9 per group. Full text read. Programme also included over/underweight ball bowling (±10–15%, 24–30 balls), done first each session.

title: Female cricket pace bowling: kinematic and anthropometric relationships with ball release speed (summarised by Clean Bowled / whit.com.au)
author: Lyons C, Felton PJ, McCabe C
publisher: South African Journal of Sports Medicine 35(1):1-5
notes: 11 high-performance (Irish international/interprovincial) female bowlers: 23.0 m/s (~83 km/h, range ~73-95) vs elite female mean 27.9 m/s (~100 km/h) from Felton 2019; run-up ~18 km/h. Later arm position at release strongest predictor; 'individual-specific optimal run-up speeds' likely based on height. Read via detailed secondary summary; journal page confirmed title only.

title: Investigating the relationships between technique parameters and ball release speed in female fast bowling (summarised by Clean Bowled / whit.com.au)
author: Felton P, Lister S, King M
publisher: 5th World Congress of Science and Medicine in Cricket (conference abstract)
notes: 18 elite female bowlers: run-up speed predicted speed (as in men), but faster women had MORE front-knee flexion at release and earlier arm - opposite to elite men; attributed to strength/technique differences (front knee collapsing). Secondary summary of a conference abstract; low weight.

title: Strength and conditioning practices for the optimisation of speed and accuracy in cricket fast bowlers: A systematic review and meta-analysis
author: Ramachandran AK, Singh U, Lathlean TJH
publisher: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching 17(5):1211-1224
notes: 10 studies (8 meta-analysed), quality low-moderate. Plyometric training: moderate significant effect on bowling speed (SMD 0.75); resistance training small non-significant (SMD 0.40); modified ball weight small non-significant (SMD 0.30). DOI 10.1177/17479541211070938. Abstract only.

title: Effect of Ball Weight on Speed, Accuracy, and Mechanics in Cricket Fast Bowling
author: Wickington KL, Linthorne NP
notes: 10 trained men; balls 46-137% of 156 g. Speed fell ~1.1 m/s per +100 g; accuracy/mechanics not adversely affected. Training with under/overweight balls may have given >1.5 m/s gains in some players. Small sample. Abstract via Europe PMC.

title: Spikes in acute workload are associated with increased injury risk in elite cricket fast bowlers
author: Hulin BT, Gabbett TJ, Blanch P, Chapman P, Bailey D, Orchard JW
notes: 28 elite bowlers, 43 seasons. Acute = 1-week, chronic = 4-week rolling average. Acute>chronic -> RR 2.1 (balls) / 2.2 (sRPE) next week. Acute >200% of chronic: RR 3.3 (balls) and 4.5 (sRPE) vs 50-99%; 150-199% internal RR 2.1. Higher chronic external workload associated with lower injury risk. Intro cites: forces up to ~8x body mass at delivery stride; Dennis 2003 window 123-188 deliveries/week (RR 1.4 below/above), <2 days (RR 2.4) or >5 days (RR 1.8) between sessions; Orchard 2009 >50 overs in a match -> injury risk 9-16% over following 14-28 days, 3-4 week delay. Full text read. DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2013-092524. Citing Dennis 2003: lowest injury risk at 3–4 days between bowling sessions (<2 days RR 2.4, >5 days RR 1.8).

title: Is bowling workload a risk factor for injury to Australian junior cricket fast bowlers?
author: Dennis RJ, Finch CF, Farhart PJ
notes: 44 junior bowlers (mean 14.7 y), one season; 25% overuse injury (7 of 11 back). Average <3.5 days between bowling days RR 3.1 (1.1-8.9); bowling >=2.5 days/week RR 2.5 (ns trend); >=50 deliveries/day RR 2.0 (ns trend). Abstract via Europe PMC.

title: Incidence and prevalence of lumbar stress fracture in English County Cricket fast bowlers, association with bowling workload and seasonal variation
author: Alway P, Brooke-Wavell K, Langley B, King M, Peirce N
notes: 368 county fast bowlers 2010-2016; 2.46 LSF per 100 bowlers/yr; 18-22 y highest (4.90/100/yr, 56% of LSFs); 74% under 25; L4/L5 most affected. Peak 7-day load 234-293 deliveries OR 11.0 vs <197; 28- and 90-day loads not significant. Recommend workload guidance for under-25s. Full text: 234–293 deliveries OR 11.0 (95% CI 2.2–55.9) but relative risk ≈3.18 (95% CI 1.68–3.86) vs <197; script uses ~3×. 93% of fractures contralateral to the bowling arm. ≥294 deliveries RR 3.06 (1.72–3.63).

title: Incidence and prevalence of elite male cricket injuries using updated consensus definitions
author: Orchard JW, Kountouris A, Sims K
publisher: Open Access Journal of Sports Medicine 7:187-194
notes: Australian elite cricket 2006-2016: fast bowler injury prevalence 20.6% vs 12.5% all players; lumbar stress fractures most prevalent injury, ~15% of all missed playing time; spikes riskier than absolute load; low loads leave players underprepared; research hasn't shown that technique coaching prospectively reduces LSF risk.

title: Are Fast-Bowlers Prone to Back Injuries? Prevalence of Lumbar Spine Injuries in Fast-Bowlers: Review of MRI-Based Studies
author: Arora M, Paoloni JA, Kandwal P, Diwan AD
notes: Narrative review of 9 MRI studies. Defines side-on, front-on, mixed (switches front-on to side-on in the delivery stride). Mixed action -> excessive lumbar extension/rotation and counter-rotation; counter-rotation cut-offs >40 deg (some studies) and >20 deg (Burnett 1996). Pars abnormalities 24-81% of bowlers; non-dominant-side pars abnormality 81% vs 36% controls (Ranson 2005). Elliott & Khangure 2002 education programme: safe technique 20% -> 67%; only 1 safe-technique bowler developed new disc degeneration vs 20 mixed. Full text via Europe PMC.

title: Risk factors and successful interventions for cricket-related low back pain: a systematic review
author: Morton S, Barton CJ, Rice S, Morrissey D
notes: 12 risk-factor studies; moderate evidence that shoulder counter-rotation (associated with mixed actions) is linked to LBP; moderate evidence that acute MRI bone stress precedes lumbar stress fracture; intervention studies too low quality for conclusions. Abstract via Europe PMC.

title: Biomechanical Evolution in Longitudinal Analysis of Lumbar Stress Injuries in Fast Bowlers: A Systematic Review
author: Arun C, Raman SA, Nimishaanth SS, Thiagarajan KA, Sivaraman A
notes: 37 studies, mostly observational. Counter-rotation >25 deg linked to higher spinal loading; mixed-action label itself inconsistently linked (73-78% of bowlers classed mixed in some cohorts; Ranson 2008 no link). Lateral trunk flexion linked to injury; straighter front knee raises shear/GRF; under-22s 3.7-6.7x bone stress risk (Blanch 2015); each year younger 2.99x; taller and faster bowlers slightly higher risk (Sims 2021). Recommends screening, workload regulation, gradual progression, lumbopelvic strength/control. No formal evidence grading.

title: Lumbar load in adolescent fast bowlers: A prospective injury study
author: Bayne H, Elliott B, Campbell A, Alderson J
publisher: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport 19(2):117-122
notes: 25 bowlers aged 14-19; 12 developed low back injury. Injured: more thorax lateral flexion at release (50 vs 40 deg), higher lumbar moments, lower back-extensor endurance (103 vs 132 s), more knee valgus in single-leg decline squat. Abstract via Europe PMC.

title: Exercise-based injury prevention for community-level adolescent cricket pace bowlers: A cluster-randomised controlled trial
author: Forrest MRL, Hebert JJ, Scott BR, Dempsey AR
publisher: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport 23(5):475-480
notes: 65 community bowlers aged 14-17; 8-week programme during twice-weekly training improved shoulder, hamstring and hip adductor strength, balance reach (~+3.6-3.8% leg length) and back endurance (+20 s). Did not measure injuries. Abstract via Europe PMC.

title: Modifying bowling kinematics in cricket pace bowlers with exercise-based injury prevention: A cluster-randomised controlled trial
author: Forrest MRL, Hebert JJ, Scott BR, Dempsey AR
publisher: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport 23(12):1172-1177
notes: Same programme: reduced shoulder counter-rotation (-3.8 deg) and lateral trunk flexion (-2.2 deg) vs control; no change in ball velocity (+1.1 km/h, ns). Abstract via Europe PMC.

title: Junior Pace Bowling Workload Guidelines
author: Cricket Australia
notes: U17 '1-3-5': rest day after each bowling day, max 3 bowling days/wk, max 5 overs/spell, 20 min between training spells. 17-19 '2-4-6': max 2 days in a row, 4 days/wk, 6 overs/spell. Match: 15-17 5 overs/spell 16/day; 17-19 6/18. Pre-season build-up 6-8 weeks (15-19), full build-up usually >10 wk. Light week every 4-6 wk; 7-10 days off every 10-12 wk; ~3 months off end of season. Back bone stress injuries often develop before pain; if a junior gets back pain while bowling, stop and see a sports doctor/physio. Higher risk 2-3 years after growth spurt; taller/faster/recently grown/previous injury need more recovery.

title: ECB Recreational Cricket Safety Regulations 2025 - Regulation 20.1 Fast Bowling (reproduced by Cornwall Cricket Board)
author: England and Wales Cricket Board
publisher: Cornwall Cricket Board (reproduction of ECB regulations)
notes: Revised limits 2025 (mandatory, age 19 and under, hardball): <=11: 4 overs/spell, 8/day; 12-13: 5/10; 14-15: 5/12; 16-17: 6/15; 18-19: 7/18. Rest after a spell until the same number of overs bowled from that end. Training deliveries at (near) match intensity count; walk-throughs/half-speed don't. Secondary copy; ECB site not opened.

title: Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio: Conceptual Issues and Fundamental Pitfalls
author: Impellizzeri FM, Tenan MS, Kempton T, Novak A, Coutts AJ
publisher: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance 15(6):907-913
notes: ACWR causal role not established; ratio has statistical artefacts and lacks rationale; authors say no evidence supports using ACWR for load-management or injury-reduction recommendations. Abstract via Europe PMC.

title: Quantifying Workload and Injury Risk Among Cricket Fast Bowlers: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
author: Chelladurai A, Raman SA, Kirthen H, et al.
notes: 33 studies; 6 cohorts pooled: elevated ACWR associated with injury RR 2.45 (1.48-4.06), I2 ~77%; ACWR ~1.4-2.0+ linked to higher incidence. High heterogeneity. Abstract via Europe PMC.

title: ACSM Position Stand: Quantity and quality of exercise... in apparently healthy adults - reviewed in 'From 1998 to 2011: ACSM Publishes Updated Exercise Guidelines'
author: Garber CE et al. (position stand); summary by Kravitz L
publisher: Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 43(7):1334-1359 / University of New Mexico
notes: Resistance: 2-3 d/wk, 48 h between sessions for the same muscles; 60-70% 1RM novice-intermediate; 8-12 reps; single set for novices, 2-4 sets for most adults; 2-3 min rest. Flexibility-injury link not substantiated. Read via summary tables.

title: The effect of plyometric training volume on jumping performance
author: Ebben WP, Suchomel TJ, Garceau LR
notes: Novice recommendation 80-100 foot contacts/session (Potach & Chu 2008; Chu & Myer 2013). Low-volume (60-100 contacts, 2x/wk, 48-96 h apart) as effective as double volume. Year not printed.

title: The effectiveness of exercise interventions to prevent sports injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
author: Lauersen JB, Bertelsen DM, Andersen LB
notes: Strength training RR 0.315 (0.207-0.480); proprioception RR 0.55; stretching RR 0.963 (no effect). Not cricket-specific. Abstract via Europe PMC.

title: Risk Factors and Successful Interventions for Cricket-Related Low Back Pain: An Updated Systematic Review
author: Singh S, Baker J, Egginton S
notes: 16 risk-factor studies (15 high quality): LBP associated with higher workload, lower bone mineral density, poor lumbopelvic control (more side flexion); MRI bone marrow oedema an early sign before stress fracture; high-quality intervention studies scarce. Abstract via Europe PMC.

title: Fastest delivery of a cricket ball (male)
author: Guinness World Records
notes: Shoaib Akhtar, 161.3 km/h (100.23 mph), England v Pakistan, Newlands, 22 Feb 2003. ICC does not officially recognise speed-gun records.
